articles.title: Woman doesn’t reply to colleague on social media—days later, she’s let go
articles.summary: Fired for being "unprofessional" online, TikTok creator Charlotte Blandford Tagg says many share her confusion.
articles.body:
A content creator who says she was fired from her job for being "unprofessional online" has told Newsweek she believes her experience is becoming increasingly common, as more employees find their off-the-clock social media presence colliding with their employer's expectations.

Charlotte Blandford Tagg, who has amassed more than 46,000 followers on TikTok , was let go from her position at a small magazine on August 27, after failing her probationary period. The reason given, she said, was straightforward. Former bosses told her she had been "unprofessional online."

"I was working as a content creator for the magazine, and I've been creating content and posting online for around four years," Blandford Tagg, from England, told Newsweek . "I was specifically dismissed for failing my probation, with the reason given being that I had been 'unprofessional online.'"

Her case has sparked upset among her followers, resonating with a wider swath of the workforce navigating the blurred line between personal expression and professional obligation.

"I think this is becoming increasingly common because people want—and often need—to earn more money than their wages allow," she said. "Single mothers in particular have huge pressures on them, and those pressures are only increasing."

Blandford Tagg's TikTok bio declares that she "likes to overshare," though her content is largely in line with the confessional, slice-of-life style that has become ubiquitous on such platforms.

Her most viral video , posted May 13, has racked up more than 1.3 million views. In it, she speaks candidly about an incident of racism connected to her son's primary school, describing how she plans to teach him that people of all ethnic backgrounds deserve equal treatment, in hopes his outlook might ripple outward to other children.

The comments section is overwhelmingly supportive, with viewers on TikTok praising her openness.

Still, Blandford Tagg acknowledged that her public account—and the attention it draws—has, at times, created friction. She said the situation leading up to her redundancy was compounded when someone who had been lined up to work for the company for free complained to her manager that Blandford Tagg had failed to respond to them, while apparently still finding time to post TikToks.

"I don't think people should have to give up their lives outside of work simply because they have a job," she said. "People should be allowed to do what they want outside of their 9–5."

The backlash to her firing, she said, reflects how deeply social media is now woven into everyday life.

"It's fun, it's community, it's a source of income and, in a world where we're constantly getting glimpses into other people's homes and minds, I think we should be entering an era where the person you are at work and the person you are online can be different," she said, adding: "However, I did work for a small-town, small-minded company, so perhaps it shouldn't have come as a huge surprise!

Blandford Tagg kept the name of her former employer private and has since joined No Shame, a PR agency start-up geared toward women who do not necessarily fit conventional notions of professionalism.

"I think the word 'professional' has sometimes become another word for 'robot,'" she said. "I don't think you should have to hide your personality or your life to be taken seriously at work."

Her situation is playing out against a backdrop of staggering platform reach. TikTok counts roughly 26.8 million users in the U.K., where Blandford Tagg is based, and 1.99 billion monthly active users worldwide, according to software company Sprout Social, while DemandSage puts the worldwide figure at 2.21 billion.

Newsweek spoke to several career experts about why conflicts like Blandford Tagg's appear to be multiplying.

Sam Wright, head of career strategy at Huntr.co, framed it as a question of control.

"Many businesses see the strong social following of an employee as an asset in today's age where attention is difficult to come by but they want it on their terms," Wright said, predicting that as audiences become currency, "more and more employees will be expected to have an audience… and this issue of who controls social media will grow."

Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, argued that the content itself often matters less than its traceability.

"A joke told to a friend is perfectly fine whereas a joke on camera is a problem," she said, describing employees with large followings as "a channel that the company can associate themselves with but has absolutely no control of."

She likened firms' attempts to police off-hours behavior to the erosion of non-compete clauses, adding that fired workers "can now reach audiences much broader than previously" by explaining why they lost their jobs .

Career strategist Michelle Enjoli said the underlying issue is one of blurred identity.

"Your online presence has become an extension of your professional reputation," she said.

Her proposed fix? Clearer, written boundaries.

"The solution is a clearer conversation that defines what's off-limits versus what's just personality," she said.

Blandford Tagg's former employer could not be reached for comment because she chose to keep their identity private.

Update 9/8/26, 11:54 a.m. ET: This article was updated with additional information.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Charlotte Nisbet and Emma Lee-Sang

articles.title: Newlywed finds out husband okayed his entire family staying 5-6 weeks in their small 2-bedroom apartment,  leaving her ready to flee to her parents
articles.summary: A freshly married couple still figuring out how to share a closet. Tiny two-bedroom apartment in furnace weather. Then a full guest list sneaks in through th...
articles.body:
A newly married couple finds themselves hosting the husband's extended family for an unexpected 5-6 week stay in their small two-bedroom apartment without prior consent.

The wife is faced with the challenge of accommodating her in-laws' strict vegetarian lifestyle and moral standards, conflicting with her own habits and beliefs in her own home.

Despite promises of respecting boundaries and partnership, the husband's lack of support and the imposition of his family's extended stay raises questions about consent and autonomy within the marriage.

A freshly married couple still figuring out how to share a closet. Tiny two-bedroom apartment in furnace weather. Then a full guest list sneaks in through the group chat. Parents-in-law, sister-in-law, her husband, and a kid. Five to six weeks. Not a long weekend not a quick visit. An entire season of television, but in real life and with zero writers

This story makes me think marriage really should come with brochures like the ones nursing homes or private schools used to have, only with an extra section titled surprise extended family residency not included, but absolutely will happen

WIBTAH if I went to stay with my parents for a couple of weeks because my husband's family planned a 5-6 week stay in our 2BHK without asking me?

This story is great and infuriating in many ways, but what I find the "funniest" is the way consent gets retrofitted after the fact. Tickets are booked, dates decided, sleeping arrangements implied, and only then does anyone casually drop how long they are staying. Apparently, the new household policy is inform not ask. Somewhere in there the phrase our home quietly shifts into his family's base camp.

Add in the lifestyle remix. The in-laws are strict vegetarians with bonus moral authority. No eggs in the house. Meanwhile, the actual residents live on non-veg and thought their kitchen was theirs. Six weeks of performing someone else's diet, dress code, and behavioral standards in what is supposed to be the safest room on the map. That is less hospitality and more low-budget re-education retreat.

Her family and friends are on the opposite side of the country. This apartment is not just a home. It is the entire social universe. Turning it into a six-week hostel run by his relatives is not a small inconvenience. It is a full-scale occupation of the only space that actually belongs to her.

For years, he sells the dream. He gets it. He respects space. He will run interference. This is the non-negotiable boundary. Then the moment arrives and the response is a shrug dressed up as diplomacy. What can he do? Everything is already booked. As if airline confirmation emails have more authority than his spouse.

The tension is not about being anti-family. It is about watching every promise of partnership fold the second his side wants something. Boundaries were discussed in theory. Now the experiment is live, and suddenly she is the only person expected to adjust.

images.caption: I (29F) got married in December (less than 3 months as of today) after being with my husband (29M) for almost 7 years.
One thing I've always been very clear about with him, both before and after marriage, is that I need my space and that decisions about people staying in our home should involve both of us.
Recently I found out that his sister, her husband, their child, and my in- laws have all booked tickets to come stay with us.
That's about 5-6 weeks. I would be more than happy to host them for 1-2 weeks but 5-6 weeks seems too overwhelming at this stage.
The part that really upset me is that no one asked me beforehand. I only found out after everything was already booked.
Stressed woman sitting on a couch with her hand on her forehead while a man sits in the background facing away after an argument.
That too when it was asked that how long they were planning to stay. We live in a 2- bedroom apartment in is an extremely hot climate, and this will mean 7 people total in the house in peak summer.
My husband will be at work most of the day, so I'll be the one at home with everyone.

articles.title: Former Connecticut official convicted of bribery asks judge to spare him prison
articles.summary: Konstantimos "Kosta" Diamantis, who is facing up to 13 years in prison for bribery, asked a judge to consider home detention instead.
articles.body:
Konstantimos "Kosta" Diamantis, a former state school construction official convicted of taking bribes, is asking a federal court for home detention and maximum probation instead of up to 13 years as prison sentencing guidelines recommend.

"Mr. Diamantis does not minimize the seriousness of the jury's verdict or his breach of the public trust," his attorney, Norm Pattis, wrote in a motion to the U.S. Judge Stefon Underhill at U.S. District Court in Bridgeport.

Diamantis is scheduled to be sentenced Sept. 17 after a jury last October found him guilty of 21 counts of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and making false statements to federal investigators.

He has been free on a $500,000 bond since his arrest several years ago and was allowed to remain on bond after his conviction.

The prosecution argued Diamantis used his position as head of the state's Office of School Construction Grants and Review to steer contracts on school projects in exchange for more than $75,000 in bribes.

In his motion, Pattis urged the court to consider all the circumstances surrounding Diamantis' crimes and the current situation of his 70-year-old client.

"He asks the Court to impose an individualized sentence based on all the circumstances rather than treating the advisory range as presumptively appropriate," Pattis said.

That sentence, Pattis continued, would not include jail time but would contain strict restrictions against future government employment or contracting, financial disclosure and monitoring, payment of restitution when appropriate and a prohibition against profiting from his crimes.

"His request rests on the combined force of his age, lack of physical dangerousness, loss of the position that enabled the conduct, financial ruin, loss of professional status, diminished earning capacity, family circumstances, and the limited additional sentencing value of a decade or more in prison," Pattis said.

Diamantis also faces a second trial, his state pension is likely to be forfeited, his $2,600 a month in social security would cease if incarcerated and future employment prospects are slight, Pattis added.

A second trial is scheduled for early next year for additional public corruption charges. Federal prosecutors claim Diamantis, who has forfeited his law license and is a former state lawmaker, quashed a state audit of an eye care practice that was engaged in healthcare fraud when he was employed in the governor's budget department, the Office of Policy and Management.

articles.title: He Bought a $3,000 Sony TV. When It Broke, Sony Threatened Him With a $500K Lawsuit
articles.summary: Sony India threatened a customer with a 5 crore rupee lawsuit after he built a website documenting his denied Bravia TV warranty claim.
articles.body:
A customer purchased a Sony Bravia TV under warranty, but when vertical green lines appeared on the screen, Sony classified it as "external damage" and demanded $307 for repair instead of honoring the warranty.

Sony responded to the customer's public criticism by sending a legal notice threatening $500K in damages if the customer did not take down a website documenting the warranty dispute.

Legal commentary suggests Sony's actions resemble strategic legal pressure to silence critics rather than resolve disputes, raising concerns about the risks of publicly criticizing corporations.

Spend $3,000 on a premium TV. Twenty-two months later, vertical green lines crawl across the screen. You're still under warranty. Sony sends a technician . The technician says: external damage. No free repair. That'll be $307, please. You document everything and build a website. Sony responds with a six-page legal notice threatening $500K in damages. This is not a hypothetical. This happened — and it raises an uncomfortable question about how much risk comes with criticizing a corporation publicly when you may already be paying too much for the privilege.

When "External Damage" Means Whatever Sony Needs It to Mean

The facts here are straightforward, which is precisely what makes them worse.

In September 2024 , a customer purchased a 55-inch Sony Bravia Mini LED TV for ₹150,031, covered by a three-year Sony warranty and a two-year extended warranty from retailer Croma, according to Navbharat Times.

Vertical green lines appeared around 22 months into ownership — well inside the warranty window.

Sony's technician classified the defect as "external damage" despite no visible dent or crack, and never provided the detailed technical report the customer repeatedly requested, per Navbharat Times.

Sony quoted ₹29,130 ($307) for panel replacement instead of honoring the warranty. Sportskeeda Tech reports the technician admitted on video that he never physically inspected the internal panel and lacked engineering qualifications.

A diagnosis made from photos, without opening the device, by someone without engineering credentials is not a diagnosis. It is a liability shield dressed up as a verdict. Worth noting: Sony has historically run free evaluation and repair programs for specific Bravia models when systemic issues emerge, per Sony's own support documentation. That generosity, apparently, has limits — not unlike the pattern seen when dealers keep recommending a $300 fix consumers never actually needed.

"The notice referenced damages of up to ₹5 crore if he did not comply." — according to Sportskeeda Tech

A $500K Crore Threat Is Not Customer Service

Sony's legal escalation arrived before its warranty dispute was ever resolved.

The customer did what anyone does in the era of viral Reddit threads and public callout posts — he documented everything. He registered SonyBravia.com, launched a site called " Sorry Bravia ," and published a full chronological timeline, photographs, and service communications. He posted "Never buy a Sony Bravia." Sony's response on September 1, 2026: a six-page legal notice demanding the site come down, the domain be surrendered, and an unconditional apology be issued — or face civil and criminal defamation proceedings, per Entertales.

Legal commentary cited by Legal Suvidha describes Sony's move as resembling SLAPP tactics — strategic legal pressure designed to silence critics rather than resolve disputes. Sony's notice reportedly argues the SonyBravia.com domain misuses its trademark and could mislead consumers into thinking they have reached an official brand page. That is a recognizable legal concern. It collapses fast, though, when Sony had not resolved a warranty claim on a ₹1.5 lakh TV before reaching for a ₹5 crore in damages legal weapon.

The customer has refused to remove the site. His consumer complaint remains pending in India's court system. The case is unresolved — and any consumer who has ever left a one-star review online may want to pay attention to how it ends, particularly anyone who has already wrestled with frustrating computer problems and the indifferent support that often follows.

articles.title: 11 European nations and Canada announce trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank
articles.summary: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank and said the UK was bringing in an "import...
articles.body:
The UK and France were among 12 countries to announce new trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, amid what they called a "rapidly deteriorating" situation marked by increasing settler attacks on Palestinians.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden joined the UK and France in confirming plans to introduce restrictions on trade with settlements, according to a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers.

"The Government of Israel's actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-State solution," the statement reads, adding that there have been "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion."

"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," it continued.

It comes after the Israeli government last month opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 housing units in the West Bank, drawing widespread condemnation from the international community and human rights groups.

The units, destined for the E1 settlement area, would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.

In their statement on Tuesday, the 12 foreign ministers called the decision to publish tenders "unacceptable."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "have agreed on the need to take action to prevent further damage," the statement added.

Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank, saying that the Israeli government had often "turned a blind eye to this."

He announced that the UK would also be bringing in an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories."

"I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," he told MPs.

In a post on X, Miliband's French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Paris had taken the decision to enforce the sanctions as the West Bank was "on the brink of explosion."

"Unchecked expansion of settlements in violation of international law, a surge in violence committed by extremist settlers against Palestinians, and acts of terror condemned by the Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote.

Burnham later issued his own statement on Tuesday evening, calling the newly announced measures "carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government."

"Before I became Prime Minister, I said our country's response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That's why I committed to changing the government's approach," the UK leader added.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on Tuesday ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem in response to the moves taken by Westminster, as he hit out at Miliband's statement.

"The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Sa'ar said.

Israel has also announced that it will henceforth refuse entry to 12 British nationals.

The list reportedly includes former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, his Your Party cofounder and MP for Coventry South Zarah Sultana, and Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington.

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.

According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.

Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.
